A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniCA, with matching core methods and extensive overlapping experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies in v2 are identifiable rather than extraction gaps.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting experiments, ablations, case studies, and five-seed evaluations across unimodal and multimodal datasets.

after.justification: V2 retains original forecasting results and adds backbone comparisons, imputation experiments, efficiency measurements, and additional ablations and analyses.

M1.justification: The homogenizer and pre/post-fusion architecture remain unchanged. Section 4.3 extends the predominantly quantile-loss treatment to backbone-specific Huber and likelihood objectives. Appendix E.4 adds an imputation adaptation using masked squared error and MOMENT's frozen reconstruction head, a limited procedural extension beyond forecasting.

E1.justification: The original 12 unimodal forecasting datasets, seven evaluated Time-MMD domains, and MMSP remain. V2 adds imputation on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Electricity, and Weather, substantially extending task coverage. Appendix G.6 also introduces evaluation with an additional uninformative noisy covariate.

E2.justification: V2 evaluates ChronosX, explicitly excluded in v1, and adds Time-MoE, MM-TSF, and ChatTime comparisons. Time-MMD gains TFT+CH and TiDE+CH variants, while imputation introduces a zero-shot MOMENT comparator. NBEATS disappears from the 12-dataset comparison but remains in the EPF comparison.

E3.justification: The new imputation protocol specifies a 6:2:2 split, 512-point windows, length-8 patches, four masking ratios, identical comparison masks, and evaluation only on masked entries. New experiments introduce backbone-freezing, covariate-gating, and noise controls. V2 also specifies a 20% Time-MMD test split while retaining the generic 10% rule from v1, leaving the actual split unresolved.

E4.justification: V2 adds efficiency measurements, pretrained-versus-adapted and frozen-versus-finetuned comparisons, static-covariate removal, covariate-gating controls, noise robustness, alternative fusion, and embedding-correlation analysis. Earlier fusion-position, text-encoder, homogenizer architecture/dimension, and case-study analyses largely remain; their relocation or redisplay is not new evidence. Image-only MMSP ablation rows are removed.

E5.justification: Appendix E.1 retains the same five seeds, {41, 42, 43, 44, 45}, and mean plus one-standard-deviation reporting. V1 Table 9 and v2 Table 7 contain identical uncertainty entries. The added experiments do not introduce new confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run reporting practices.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial comparator, imputation, efficiency, and control results, while shared forecasting scores largely remain unchanged. Image-only MMSP results from v1 Tables 1 and 14 disappear. Some revised summaries conflict with retained tables: v2 Figure 3b gives TiDE+CH MMSP MAE as 0.306, whereas v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 11 both give 0.206; this is not an established performance deterioration.

T1.justification: The problem formulation and fusion mathematics retain their substance; replacing CondAttnPool/BMM notation with CAP and matrix multiplication is equivalent. Metric definitions remain unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. The objective extensions concern the method rather than new theoretical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: homogenizing heterogeneous covariates, integrating them through attention-based fusion with frozen TSFMs, and supporting compatibility, universality, and preserved forecasting ability. Rewording and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning covariate information versus parameter count, the importance of nonlinear gated fusion, resistance to irrelevant inputs, and temporal structure in homogenized embeddings. Appendix E.4 extends the applicability discussion beyond forecasting. The original temporal-alignment and noisy-covariate limitations are retained essentially verbatim in Appendix I.

D1.justification: V2 adds an anonymous code-access option and dependency-location information, explicit backbone context lengths, a ChatTime checkpoint, and Time-MoE architecture details. These extend documentation rather than establish changes to the retained implementation. Hardware, preprocessing, optimization, and hyperparameter-search information largely match v1.

R1.justification: V2 adds references and discussion for MiTSformer, ChatTime, and Huber loss, and sharpens the distinction between UniCA and ChronosX's point-wise applicability. The broader research positioning remains stable. Time-MoE and MOMENT were already cited in v1; their new evaluation is not a new citation.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title and author list, revises several explanatory passages, adds an appendix contents list and ethics/reproducibility statements, and moves limitations to Appendix I while removing the NeurIPS checklist. The core narrative, method organization, and much of the existing appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 consolidates main benchmark summaries into the three-panel Figure 3, reorganizes analysis panels, and expands numerous comparison displays. The MMSP and homogenizer-comparison tables are merged into appendix Table 11, and new imputation, control, efficiency, and correlation displays are added. Existing case-study figures are largely retained.

improvement.justification: The added imputation experiment, ChronosX comparison, and mechanism controls materially strengthen validation. However, v2 introduces important numerical inconsistencies: Figure 3a labels Time-MoE MAE values as MAPE relative to Table 8, and Section 5.2 claims a 5.9% Chronos-Bolt MMSP improvement while Table 11 retains MAE 0.193 for both zero-shot and UniCA. Broader evidence therefore coexists with reduced reporting reliability, preventing a confident net quality judgment.
